legacy_report:
SOURCE: "MEMO: Memory as a Model", Quek, Lee, Leong, Verma, Prakash, Chen, Low, Rus, Solar-Lezama (NUS, A*STAR, MIT, Liquid AI, others). arXiv:2605.15156v2 [cs.CL], 20 May 2026. Preprint (no venue printed).
COVERAGE: Read all 105,610 chars (main text, all appendices A-O, tables 1-20, Figs 2-5 text). References skimmed only.

IMPORTANT FIT WARNING: This is NOT agent memory or learning from experience. MEMO is "knowledge integration": a small fine-tuned "memory model" absorbs a static document corpus, and a frozen "executive" LLM queries it. No agent trajectories, no raw-vs-distilled experience memory, no full-context baseline. Closest fit: distilled-into-weights memory vs RAG over raw documents, with a cost angle.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. A fine-tuned 14B memory model beats retrieval baselines on NarrativeQA and MuSiQue, and ties them on BrowseComp-Plus.
 number: NarrativeQA 26.85% vs HippoRAG2 21.39%, NV-Embed-V2 20.59% (Qwen2.5-32B executive); Gemini-3-Flash 53.58% vs 26.62% best baseline. MuSiQue 48.30 vs 42.17. BrowseComp-Plus 54.22 vs HippoRAG2 56.11 (Qwen), 66.67 vs 66.33 (Gemini).
 setup: 300 BrowseComp-Plus Qs (3,541 docs), 293 NarrativeQA Qs (105 docs per text; the paper's footnote says 10 docs), 1,000 MuSiQue Qs (5,296 docs). Memory model Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, best epoch. Qwen runs are mean of 3; Gemini is a single run. Judge: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite.
 quote: "On NarrativeQA, the most challenging benchmark (App. I), MEMO achieves 26.85% with Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and 53.58% with Gemini-3-Flash, substantially surpassing all baselines."
 where: Sec 5.1, Table 2, ~p8
2. Retrieval degrades with distractors; the memory model does not.
 number: adding 1x distractor documents: NV-Embed-V2 and HippoRAG2 drop 6.22 points on BrowseComp-Plus; MEMO +0.55 (BrowseComp-Plus) and -1.77 (MuSiQue).
 setup: Qwen2.5-32B executive. At 2x distractors HippoRAG2 loses 11.55 points on BrowseComp-Plus (Table 17). Note that at 0 distractors HippoRAG2 (62.33) beats MEMO (53.67) on BrowseComp-Plus.
 quote: "MEMO maintains stable performance across both benchmarks, with a marginal improvement of 0.55% on BrowseComp-Plus and a decline of only 1.77% on MuSiQue, both within one standard deviation"
 where: Sec 5.2, Table 3, App L Table 17
3. Cross-document synthesis of the training data is the key ingredient. Distilling the corpus into QA "reflections" matters more than raw text.
 number: removing Step 5 drops NarrativeQA 24.00 to 6.37 and MuSiQue 42.90 to 24.17.
 setup: leave-one-out ablation, 1.5B memory model, Qwen2.5-32B executive, 3 runs.
 quote: "Its removal causes accuracy to collapse to 6.37% and 24.17% on NarrativeQA and MuSiQue respectively, against baseline scores of 24.00% and 42.90%"
 where: App E.1, Table 9. Removing Step 3 (self-containment filter) raised NarrativeQA to 28.90 (the authors give a domain-specific explanation).
4. Training cost is large. This is the main cost of the approach.
 number: data generation ~240/200/150 GPU-hours and 14B training ~180/150/90 GPU-hours (BrowseComp-Plus/NarrativeQA/MuSiQue). The reflection datasets hold 1.64M / 1.28M / 0.66M QA pairs, so one memory model costs about 330-420 GPU-hours on BrowseComp-Plus.
 quote: "Generating the full reflection dataset for BrowseComp-Plus, NarrativeQA, and MuSiQue took approximately 240, 200, and 150 GPU-hours respectively."
 where: App G
5. Model merging for incremental updates saves compute but costs accuracy.
 number: 33% less compute at K=2 (48 vs 72 8xH100 GPU-hours). Accuracy falls from 26.85 to 15.81 (Qwen) and from 53.58 to 34.47 (Gemini). The 14 configurations range from 7.85 to 15.81.
 setup: NarrativeQA split in two, ~640k pairs each, TIES rho=0.3 (best of the sweep).
 quote: "Merge-TIES (ρ=0.3) trails the full-retrain MEMORY model by 11.0% under Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and 19.1% under Gemini-3-Flash"
 where: Sec 5.5, Table 6, Table 12
6. Multi-turn, structured querying beats single-turn querying.
 number: BrowseComp-Plus 32.56 (single turn) vs 54.22 (structured). MuSiQue 37.57 vs 48.30.
 setup: same memory model, Qwen executive.
 where: App J.2, Table 16. Unstructured multi-turn plateaus: 47.33 at 15 turns and 48.67 at 50 turns on BrowseComp-Plus.
 Also: LoRA is much worse than full SFT. On the Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct memory model, BrowseComp-Plus is 48.78 vs 54.22 (Table 20). LoRA nearly fails on LFM2.5, at 0.78 on BrowseComp-Plus.

BASELINES AND MATCHING
- Baselines are BM25, NV-Embed-V2, HippoRAG2 (top-k=9 with adaptive backoff) and Cartridges (a trained KV cache; it scores 0.00 / 3.75 / 8.57, so it is a weak or possibly poorly tuned baseline). Perfect Retrieval gives the upper bound: 79.67 / 51.42 / 62.83 with Qwen.
- A no-context baseline is given only in App I (Qwen: 0.00 / 5.35 / 17.03; Gemini: 1.33 / 26.62 / 41.80). There is NO full-context baseline, and no simple-RAG-vs-agent-memory comparison.
- Compute and tokens are NOT matched. The paper never reports executive-side token counts, only the interaction budgets. MEMO uses 1 grounding + 7 entity-ID + 8 answer-seeking turns, so up to 16 executive-memory exchanges. Retrieval baselines appear to be single-shot. The paper itself says "alternative settings may yield similar performance with greater token efficiency." Its inference-cost claim ("retrieval cost independent of corpus size") is asserted, not measured. The training GPU-hours (hundreds) are not compared with baseline indexing cost.
- HippoRAG2 numbers differ from the original paper because it was rerun with a Qwen2.5-32B reader instead of Llama3.3-70B.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: upfront training per corpus; performance may vary across domains and LLM families; a fixed-size memory model is bounded by capacity and may fail on large or dense corpora; Step 5 data generation scales quadratically.
- Not shown: any agent or experience setting, dynamic or streaming corpora (merging is tested only at K=2 on one dataset), forgetting inside the memory model, and wall-clock latency.
- Corpora are small: ≤5.3k documents, and distractors were subsampled for cost.
- The Gemini results are a single run. Gains for the memory model over some baselines on BrowseComp-Plus are within noise, and it loses to HippoRAG2 with the Qwen executive.
- Questions are the same ones the memory corpus was built around. The training data is generated from the evaluation corpus, per question group (the "document groups" G). BrowseComp-Plus and MuSiQue groups are defined per question. This makes the setting closer to an oracle grouping than a deployable one. This is my reading of App D Table 8 ("each question is associated with a subset of chunks"), not a stated limitation.
- Dated: Qwen2.5 and Gemini-3-Flash, as of 2026.

BUILDS ON
- HippoRAG / HippoRAG2 (Gutierrez et al., NeurIPS 2024; "From RAG to memory", ICML 2025)
- NV-Embed (Lee et al., 2024)
- BM25 (Robertson & Walker, SIGIR 1994)
- Cartridges ([65])
- Latent memory: AutoCompressor (Chevalier et al., EMNLP 2023), Gist tokens (Mu et al., NeurIPS 2023), ICAE (Ge et al., ICLR 2024)
- Reversal curse work, SFT-memorizes (Chu et al., 2025)
- Fine-tuning vs retrieval (Ovadia et al., EMNLP 2024)
- Physics of LMs 3.1 (Allen-Zhu & Li, ICML 2024)
- Model merging: TIES (Yadav et al., NeurIPS 2023), DARE (Yu et al., ICML 2024), task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., ICLR 2023)
- Benchmarks: BrowseComp-Plus, NarrativeQA, MuSiQue
- MemGen (Zhang et al., ICLR 2026) is cited as latent memory for self-evolving agents.

CODE: none in the text (code is said to be in supplementary materials). Algorithm 1 (reflection QA pipeline) is on p4-5.

FIGURE (one candidate): Figure 2 (App H, p22), "Cost-accuracy trade-off on NarrativeQA when a second corpus arrives (K=2...)". It shows merge vs retrain cost against accuracy, with retrieval baselines marked. It makes the cost-accuracy tradeoff visible. Figure 1 (p2) is the pipeline overview.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is clean apart from some math symbols and Fig. 1 label text. Figures 3-5 (accuracy vs epoch) are not readable as text; the paper says peak accuracy is at epoch 2 for most models. There are no embedded instructions. The text of Sec 5 mentions "105 documents" for NarrativeQA but the footnote says 10 documents; a possible typo in the paper.
